brief: Should a consumer note-taking app move from a one-off purchase to a subscription?

steps.text:

1. What do pricing and revenue outcomes look like when consumer note-taking and productivity apps move from a one-off purchase to a subscription?
2. How do users react to these moves (churn, backlash, review ratings), and what do they say they prefer?
3. What are the benchmarks for subscription conversion, retention and LTV in consumer productivity apps?
4. Which hybrid models (for example, lifetime option, paid upgrades, sync-only subscription) have worked in note-taking?

answer:
# Decision Brief: Should a consumer note-taking app move from a one-off purchase to a subscription?

## Executive Summary
Move to a subscription only if you have ongoing costs (cloud sync, AI, storage) or a roadmap that keeps delivering value. Do it as a hybrid, not a hard switch. Keep a one-time or lifetime option, and grandfather existing buyers. The category leaders Notability and Goodnotes both ended up with hybrids after backlash or user pushback.

## Key Findings

### 1. What happened when note-taking apps made this move?
- Notability switched to a subscription and faced "substantial blowback". Users learned that features they had bought would stop working after a year. The company then reversed course and promised existing buyers lifetime access to the features they had purchased ([MacRumors forum](https://forums.macrumors.com/threads/notability-changes-app-subscription-policy-promises-existing-users-lifetime-access-to-purchased-features.2321538/page-3)).
- Goodnotes 6 launched with a subscription alongside a one-time option. Some long-time users complained that the one-time purchase lost features, and at least one user said they refunded ([MPU Talk](https://talk.macpowerusers.com/t/goodnotes-6-new-version-new-payment-models/34474)).
- Today the two have effectively swapped positions. Notability sells a one-time $49.99 option, and Goodnotes sells a one-time "Special Edition" on Apple devices ([Paperlike](https://paperlike.com/blogs/paperlikers-insights/app-review-goodnotes-vs-notability), [Goodnotes Support](https://support.goodnotes.com/hc/en-us/articles/13808767840015-Compare-Goodnotes-Plans-and-Features)).

### 2. How do users react, and what do they prefer?
- Users resent losing something they feel they own. Evernote's price increases also drew strong complaints, with one user saying they were "doubling my price to let me keep what I already have" ([TidBITS Talk](https://talk.tidbits.com/t/evernote-2026-price-tiers-floored-me/33792)).
- Lifetime licences are a real competitive threat. UpNote sells one for $39.99, and a competitor concedes it pays for itself against Evernote Starter in about five months ([Harbor](https://harbor.my/vs/upnote-vs-evernote)).
- I found no rigorous survey data on user preference. This evidence comes from forums and reviews.

### 3. What do subscription benchmarks look like for productivity apps?
Source: [RevenueCat State of Subscription Apps 2026](https://www.revenuecat.com/state-of-subscription-apps).
- Productivity yearly retention is strong at 85.6%. Monthly retention is weak at 28.2%, about 11 points below the benchmark.
- Median yearly revenue per payer is $24.95, which is mid-tier.
- Most productivity subscribers choose monthly plans (59–68%), the plan type that retains worst. Annual plans generate about 2x the revenue per install of monthly plans.
- Hard paywalls convert about 5x better than freemium (10.7% vs 2.1%), with similar retention. A paywall does cut free-user reach, and freemium gets more App Store visibility.
- Median Day-14 revenue per install in productivity is only $0.22.

### 4. What do hybrid models offer, and what does one-time pricing cost?
- A founder account on [Indie Hackers](https://www.indiehackers.com/post/subscriptions-vs-one-time-payments-a-developers-honest-take-f153e48960) says subscribers paid several times more over time than one-time buyers. It also says paid annual upgrades nearly doubled the LTV of one-time buyers. This is anecdotal.
- One-time pricing has a cost problem when cloud sync is involved. UpNote caps attachments at 20 MB and reduces image resolution to keep its lifetime licence viable ([Harbor](https://harbor.my/vs/upnote-vs-evernote)).
- Bear gates sync behind its subscription, at $2.99/month or $29.99/year ([Fabric](https://fabric.so/comparison/craft-vs-bear)). Obsidian charges for Sync ($4–5/month) and keeps the core app free ([Atlas](https://www.atlasworkspace.ai/blog/obsidian-vs-evernote)). Both tie recurring fees to recurring costs.

## Trade-offs
| Factor | Stay one-time | Full subscription | Hybrid (sub + lifetime/one-time, or paid sync) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue predictability | Low, with launch spikes | High | Medium-high |
| LTV potential | Capped unless you charge for upgrades | Highest if retained | High, with a floor from lifetime buyers |
| Covers ongoing server/AI costs | Poorly | Well | Well |
| User goodwill | High | Risky; backlash precedent | Moderate, if existing buyers are grandfathered |
| Conversion friction | Low | Higher | Medium |
| Competitive position | Matches UpNote-style lifetime offers | Exposed to lifetime and free rivals | Flexible |
| Ongoing obligation to ship | Low | High | Medium-high |

## Recommendation
**Move to a hybrid model.**
- **Subscribe for the parts that cost you money:** sync, storage and AI.
- **Grandfather existing buyers** on the features they bought.
- **Keep a priced one-time or lifetime tier** for the core offline app.
- **Push annual plans**, because monthly retention in productivity is weak.

Stay one-time only if the app is offline-only, has no AI or sync costs, and has a small team. In that case, consider paid major-version upgrades instead.

**Confidence: Medium.** The Notability and Goodnotes precedents and the RevenueCat benchmarks are consistent. Confidence is held back because there is no rigorous data on user preference. RevenueCat benchmarks also cover all productivity apps, not note-taking specifically, and they come from apps that already use subscriptions. They say nothing about converting an existing one-time user base.

## Caveats & Assumptions
- I assumed an existing paying base, some cloud or AI costs, and a roadmap that keeps shipping.
- I didn't find your app's own data. Your existing buyer count, current revenue per user, and cost to serve would change this. If most revenue comes from new-user sales and churn would be low, a subscription looks better.
- The Notability reversal details come from a forum thread quoting MacRumors, not the primary announcement.
- Several sources are vendor comparison pages (Harbor, Paperlike), which may be biased.
- The indie founder claims are anecdotal.
